title: Your creature, on screen
description: A blank page becomes a card with a creature, a name and a coloured frame - and a user interface turns out to be a tree of things with properties.

steps.title: What you are about to build
steps.body:
## Your creature, on screen

By the end of this you will have a card on the page with a creature on it and a name underneath it.

That is worth half an hour because of what it shows you. A user interface is not a drawing. It is a **tree** - things sitting inside other things - and every one of those things has **properties** you set. Once you can see a screen that way, every screen you ever build here is the same shape.

The page already has an empty shell on it. Everything inside it is yours.

steps.title: Add the card
steps.body:
Add a **Group** node inside **Page shell**, and rename it `Card`.

A Group is a container: it holds other things. It draws nothing at all by itself, which is why the page still looks empty. You have just made the box that everything else goes into.
steps.detail: Nodes come from the node picker, and you can filter it by typing the name of the node you want. To put a node *inside* another one, drop it onto that node rather than onto empty canvas - where a node lands in the tree is what decides where it appears on screen.

steps.title: Make it look like a card
steps.body:
Select `Card` and set two of its properties:

- **Size Mode** to **Content Size**
- **Background Color** to any colour you like

The size mode is the one that matters. A Group is **100% wide and 100% tall** until you tell it otherwise, so a brand-new one fills the entire screen. Content Size tells it to be exactly as big as whatever is inside it - which is what makes a card a card rather than a wall.
steps.detail: A node's properties appear in the panel on the right when you select it. **Size Mode** is in the **Dimensions** group; **Background Color** is in the **Style** group. Any colour will do here - the lesson checks that you set one, not which one you picked.

steps.title: Put the creature in the card
steps.body:
Add a **Circle** node inside `Card` and rename it `Creature`. Give it a **Size** and a **Fill Color**.

Notice that you dropped it *into* the Card, not onto the page. That is the tree doing its work: the circle is drawn inside the card because that is where it sits.
steps.detail: Circle's **Size** is in the **Dimensions** group and **Fill Color** is in the **Style** group. If the circle turns up outside the card instead of inside it, it was dropped onto the page by mistake - drag it onto `Card` and it will move.

steps.title: Give it a name
steps.body:
Add a **Text** node inside `Card`, underneath the circle, and rename it `Name`. Type your creature's name into its **Text** property.

Call it whatever you like. It is your creature, and it is going to be here for the next eleven lessons.
steps.detail: **Text** is the first property in the panel. The order of the children inside `Card` is the order they are drawn in, so if the name comes out above the circle rather than below it, drag it below the circle and it will swap.

steps.title: What you just learned
steps.body:
You built a tree.

`Page shell` holds `Card`. `Card` holds `Creature` and `Name`. Nothing here was positioned by dragging it around a canvas - each thing is drawn where it sits in that tree, and everything you can see about it is a **property** you set.

Three things worth keeping:

- **A Group is a container.** It is how you hold things together so they can be spaced, coloured and moved as one.
- **A new Group fills its parent.** 100% by 100%, until you say otherwise. A surprising number of "why does my layout look like that" moments start right here.
- **Properties are just values.** Right now you typed them in by hand. Later you will wire them to things that change - and that is the moment this stops being a picture and starts being an app.

Your creature currently ignores you completely. That is the next lesson.
